doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Joining Gerry Mulligan's band and learning from Brookmeyer
summary: Raph describes a milestone: getting Mulligan's number from Dick Hickson, calling him and sitting next to Bob Brookmeyer. He explains what he learned and what 'playing outside your instrument' means.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Right. When you think back early in your career, was there certain milestones that you reflect on now that were important, as like Gerry Mulligan or—

Very much so. I came into the business with the ability to play the trombone. I played a Broadway show, I did the music hall, I did the operas and the classical music. I did do Larry Elgart, on bass trombone by the way so I was playing first trombone on the classical end of it and I was playing bass trombone on the jazz end let’s say, not really jazz at that point but on the dance band end of it. When — a tremendous milestone was Gerry Mulligan. I remember walking, I was at the union and Dick Hickson, who is a bass trombone player, a very busy one in those days, happened to be on the same path as me. And we said hello and he looked and he said, “Oh yeah, you play bass trombone too, don’t you?” He said, “You know Gerry Mulligan is putting a band together” you know so I said, “well do you happen to have his number?” He says, “Yeah as a matter of fact I do.” So he gave me his number and I said, “Would you mind very much if I used your name as a reference?” “Yeah you can use my name.” So I called up Gerry that night, from Staten Island where I was living. And I told him who I was. He said, “Well where have you played?” I said, “Oh well, I played with Larry Elgart.” He says, “Well this is a

jazz band.” I said, “Well I’m quick.” He says, “Come on down.” That was it. That was the end of the conversation. I went down to the rehearsal. I sat next to Brookmeyer. Now Gerry, letting me into his band was a big moment for me. Because I stayed with the band for three years, I re-joined the band eighteen years later and stayed for another year or so, and musically it was a wonderful experience. Brookmeyer was the person in my life that I learned the most from. Sitting next to Bob. I always prided myself on my reading ability. I was a good reader. I could read music, and at sight, and balance and blend and listen beyond the horn and all of that. And I sat down next to Brookmeyer and it was like I couldn’t read at all. He would not only read a new arrangement, let’s say a George Russell complex arrangement, but he would read it the first time down in the style that the band was going to play after they played it twenty-five times or so. But Bob would do it right at the opening. He would do the right inflections with the right style, with the right nuances. And I can’t say I never heard him make a mistake, but I can’t recall him making a mistake. And sitting next to him from the first rehearsal on I had the ability to play outside of my instrument. So I was playing his instrument. Whatever he did I phrased the same way. And he was playing first trombone. It was interesting because it was valve trombone on first, slide trombone on second, and bass trombone on third. Wayne Andre was the slide trombone. Whatever Brookmeyer did I would do it as quick as I could so that it would almost seem I were doing it too. I would just listen intently. I was playing through his horn. And I learned a lot.
Sorry to interrupt, is that what you mean by playing outside your instrument?

Yeah. Playing your instrument means you’re involved with the instrument, the intonation, trying to fit in, trying to get the right sound and loud and soft and fast and slow and all of that. Playing outside of your instrument means almost like looking at yourself from beyond yourself and seeing how you fit in, realizing when you have the melody, when you don’t have the melody, when you have a leading line, when you should not be heard, and when it’s completely unimportant whether you play or not. I always choose not to play in those cases. But there are many, many times where it just doesn’t matter. You hear yourself being doubled over here and over there — I’m not talking about Mulligan’s band now, I’m just talking about average commercial. And there are many times that if you drop a note or two it absolutely doesn’t matter a bit. Nobody’s going to even care much less say anything. So you are hearing beyond what you’re doing. There are people though that live, eat and breathe the trombone. And everything they do is through the trombone. And there are some good musicians that do it that way too. Brookmeyer goes beyond that. He’s a superb player and what was interesting, what I learned, one of the things I learned from him in jazz playing you never knew where he was going to come in from.
